title: PostgreSQL: databases, tables and types
goal: Install PostgreSQL, use psql, and design tables with the right types and constraints.

concepts: Why a relational database: structure, constraints, transactions, queries
Installing PostgreSQL; psql basics: \l, \c, \dt, \d table, \q
CREATE DATABASE and CREATE TABLE
Types: integer, bigint, serial/identity, text, varchar, boolean, numeric, date, timestamptz, uuid, jsonb
Constraints: PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT
Keeping schema in a .sql file you can re-run

build.task: Install PostgreSQL 16+ (or run it in Docker if you prefer). Create a database taskmanager. In api-starter, create db/schema.sql for projects (id uuid PK with default gen_random_uuid(), name unique, created_at timestamptz default now()) and tasks (id uuid, project_id uuid, title, status with a CHECK of todo/doing/done, priority CHECK low/medium/high, due_date date nullable, created_at, updated_at). Run it with psql -f. Then deliberately try inserts that break each constraint (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK) and save the error messages with explanations in docs/constraints.md.
acceptance: PostgreSQL installed; database taskmanager exists
db/schema.sql creates both tables and can be re-run (DROP IF EXISTS or IF NOT EXISTS)
Correct types chosen: uuid ids, timestamptz times, date for due_date
CHECK constraints on status and priority; UNIQUE on project name
docs/constraints.md shows at least 4 real constraint errors with explanations

hints: Connect: psql -U postgres, then CREATE DATABASE taskmanager; and \c taskmanager. Run a file: psql -d taskmanager -f db/schema.sql.
On PostgreSQL 13+, gen_random_uuid() is built in: id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid().
Use timestamptz (with time zone) for moments in time, and date for calendar days like due dates.

explainBack.q: Why put rules like CHECK and UNIQUE in the database when the API already validates?
Why timestamptz instead of timestamp for created_at?

lastHintExplanation: API validation can be bypassed by a script, a bug or two requests racing each other. Database constraints are the last line of defence and keep data valid no matter who writes it. timestamptz stores an absolute moment (converted to UTC internally), so times stay correct across servers and users in different time zones.

Then write db/queries-day98.sql with 15 numbered queries and a comment above each saying what it answers: e.g. overdue tasks, tasks due this week, high-priority tasks not done, titles containing 'fix' (case-insensitive), page 2 of tasks sorted by due date (nulls last), tasks with no due date, mark all overdue tasks as high priority (inside a transaction you roll back first, then commit), delete done tasks older than 30 days, and so on. Run each and paste a short result summary as a comment.

15 queries, each with a comment saying what question it answers
Uses WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT/OFFSET, ILIKE, IS NULL, IN and BETWEEN
At least 2 UPDATE and 1 DELETE with RETURNING, all with WHERE clauses
One transaction rolled back on purpose, then re-run and committed

hints: Overdue: WHERE due_date < CURRENT_DATE AND status <> 'done'. This week: due_date BETWEEN CURRENT_DATE AND CURRENT_DATE + 6.
Nulls last: ORDER BY due_date ASC NULLS LAST. Page 2 with 10 per page: LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10.
Safety habit: write the SELECT with your WHERE first, check the rows, then turn it into UPDATE/DELETE with the same WHERE.

explainBack.q: What happens if you run UPDATE tasks SET status = 'done' without WHERE? How do you protect yourself?
Why can't you use = NULL to find rows with no due date?
lookFor: comparisons with NULL return NULL, not true

lastHintExplanation: Without WHERE, UPDATE and DELETE hit every row in the table. Write the SELECT with your WHERE first, check the rows, and run risky changes inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK until you're sure. NULL means 'unknown', so NULL = NULL isn't true; any comparison with NULL gives NULL. Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL.

predict.why: = NULL is never true; use IS NULL.

title: Relationships and JOINs
goal: Connect tables with foreign keys and combine them with JOINs.

concepts: One-to-many: tasks.project_id REFERENCES projects(id)
ON DELETE CASCADE vs RESTRICT vs SET NULL
Many-to-many with a join table (task_tags)
INNER JOIN: only matching rows
LEFT JOIN: all rows from the left, NULLs where no match
Table aliases and selecting columns from both tables

build.task: Update db/schema.sql: add the foreign key tasks.project_id → projects(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, a tags table (id, name unique) and a task_tags join table (task_id, tag_id, composite primary key, both FKs with CASCADE). Seed tags and links. Write db/queries-day99.sql with 10 queries: tasks with their project names (INNER JOIN); all projects with their tasks including empty projects (LEFT JOIN); tasks with a given tag; each task with a comma-separated list of its tags (string_agg); projects that have no tasks; and so on. Prove CASCADE works by deleting a project inside a transaction and counting tasks before and after, then rolling back.
acceptance: Foreign keys with explicit ON DELETE behaviour
Many-to-many via task_tags with a composite primary key
Inserting a task with a non-existent project_id fails (show the error)
10 join queries, including at least 3 LEFT JOINs and one 'no matches' query
CASCADE demonstrated in a rolled-back transaction

hints: Projects without tasks: SELECT p.* FROM projects p LEFT JOIN tasks t ON t.project_id = p.id WHERE t.id IS NULL;
Tags per task: SELECT t.title, string_agg(g.name, ', ' ORDER BY g.name) AS tags FROM tasks t LEFT JOIN task_tags tt ON tt.task_id = t.id LEFT JOIN tags g ON g.id = tt.tag_id GROUP BY t.id, t.title;
Composite key: PRIMARY KEY (task_id, tag_id) stops the same tag being linked twice to one task.
proof: Commit with the updated schema and queries.

explainBack.q: When did you need LEFT JOIN instead of INNER JOIN? Use one of your queries.
lookFor: when rows without matches must still appear

explainBack.q: What does ON DELETE CASCADE do, and when might it be dangerous?
lookFor: can remove lots of data unexpectedly
RESTRICT prevents deleting parents with children

lastHintExplanation: INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match on both sides, so a project with no tasks disappears. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills the right side with NULLs when there's no match, which also lets you find 'rows with no match' using WHERE right.id IS NULL. CASCADE deletes children with the parent: convenient, but one DELETE can remove far more data than expected.

title: Aggregates, GROUP BY and indexes
goal: Summarise data with aggregates and make queries fast with the right indexes.

concepts: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX; COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)
GROUP BY and the rule: selected columns must be grouped or aggregated
HAVING filters groups (WHERE filters rows)
FILTER (WHERE ...) for conditional counts
Indexes: what they are, when they help, their cost on writes
EXPLAIN ANALYZE: Seq Scan vs Index Scan

resources.title: Use The Index, Luke (SQL indexing guide)

build.task: Write db/queries-day100.sql with: tasks per project with counts per status in one row each (COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'done')), completion percentage per project, projects with more than 5 open tasks (HAVING), average days overdue for overdue tasks, and the busiest tag. Then generate 200,000 fake tasks with generate_series, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on 'tasks for one project ordered by due_date', add an index on (project_id, due_date), run it again, and record both plans and timings in docs/indexes.md with your explanation.
acceptance: Per-project summary in one query using FILTER
HAVING used correctly to filter groups
200k rows generated with generate_series
EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after the index shows Seq Scan → Index Scan and a faster time
docs/indexes.md explains why the index helps and what it costs

hints: Fake rows: INSERT INTO tasks (project_id, title, status, priority, due_date) SELECT (SELECT id FROM projects ORDER BY random() LIMIT 1), 'Task ' || g, (ARRAY['todo','doing','done'])[1 + floor(random()*3)::int], 'medium', CURRENT_DATE + (random()*60)::int FROM generate_series(1, 200000) g; (the project subquery runs once, so all rows go to one project; that's fine, or mix it up with a CASE).
CREATE INDEX tasks_project_due_idx ON tasks (project_id, due_date); then ANALYZE tasks; before re-running EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
The column order in a composite index matters: (project_id, due_date) helps 'WHERE project_id = ? ORDER BY due_date', but not 'WHERE due_date = ?' on its own.

explainBack.q: WHERE vs HAVING: explain with one of your queries.
Why not add an index on every column?
lookFor: only help queries that use them

lastHintExplanation: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters whole groups after aggregates are calculated, which is why HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 works and WHERE COUNT(*) > 5 doesn't. An index is a sorted structure that lets Postgres jump to matching rows instead of scanning the table. Every insert and update must maintain it too, so add indexes for real query patterns only.

title: Connecting Express to PostgreSQL with pg
goal: Replace your in-memory repos with PostgreSQL using parameterised queries, and understand SQL injection.

concepts: node-postgres (pg): Pool, pool.query(text, values)
Parameterised queries ($1, $2) vs string concatenation
SQL injection: what it is and how parameters prevent it
Mapping snake_case rows to camelCase objects
pg returns COUNT/bigint and numeric as strings: cast in SQL or convert
Transactions with a dedicated client (BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK)
Simple migrations: numbered .sql files applied in order

resources.title: OWASP: SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet

build.task: In api-starter: npm i pg (and -D @types/pg). Add DATABASE_URL to config. Create src/db.ts with a Pool and a tiny query<T>() helper. Move schema into db/migrations/001_init.sql and 002_tags.sql and write a scripts/migrate.ts that applies unapplied migrations in order, recording them in a schema_migrations table. Implement PostgresProjectsRepo and PostgresTasksRepo (same interfaces as before), including filtering, whitelisted sorting and pagination with a total count, all with parameters. Creating a task with tags must run in a transaction. Your Angular app should keep working unchanged.
acceptance: Every query uses $1-style parameters; no user input is concatenated into SQL
npm run migrate applies migrations once and is safe to re-run
Repos implement the same interfaces; services and controllers unchanged
List endpoint returns correct data and meta from SQL (LIMIT/OFFSET plus a COUNT)
Task + tags creation is atomic (prove rollback by forcing an error)
Angular frontend works against the PostgreSQL-backed API

hints: Dynamic filters: build arrays of SQL fragments and values together: if (status) { values.push(status); where.push(`status = $${values.length}`); }. Sort columns come from your whitelist map, never from raw input.

Transaction: const client = await pool.connect(); try { await client.query('BEGIN'); ...; await client.query('COMMIT'); } catch (e) { await client.query('ROLLBACK'); throw e; } finally { client.release(); }
COUNT(*) comes back as a string (bigint). Use COUNT(*)::int in SQL.
proof: Commit with db.ts, migrations, migrate script and Postgres repos.

explainBack.q: Show how SQL injection would work against a concatenated query, and why $1 prevents it.
lookFor: input like ' OR 1=1 -- changes the query's meaning
parameters are sent separately from SQL text
database treats them as values, never code

explainBack.q: Why didn't the services and controllers need to change when you switched to PostgreSQL?
lookFor: they depend on the repo interface

lastHintExplanation: With concatenation, input like x' OR '1'='1 becomes part of the SQL and changes what the query does. With $1 parameters, the SQL text and the values travel separately, so the database always treats input as data, never as code. Because services only depend on the repo interface, swapping the in-memory Map for Postgres changed one layer.
